title: Acts 26:1–18
context: Given permission to speak, Paul tells King Agrippa that he has lived as a strict Pharisee and now stands on trial for the hope promised to the fathers, asking why it should seem incredible that God raises the dead. He describes how he once fiercely persecuted the saints, then recounts the light from heaven on the Damascus road and Jesus’ commission: to be a servant and witness, sent to the Gentiles to open their eyes, turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, so that they receive forgiveness and a place among those sanctified by faith in Jesus.

verses.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand, and made his defense.
verses.arminianNotes: Agrippa grants permission, and Paul stretches out his hand, the orator’s gesture, and begins his defense.
verses.reformedNotes: This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts and the most fully shaped as a courtroom speech.

verses.text: “I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I am to make my defense before you today concerning all the things the Jews accuse me of,
verses.arminianNotes: Paul counts himself fortunate to make his defense before Agrippa against all the Jewish accusations.
verses.reformedNotes: His courtesy is sincere: here at last is a judge who understands the questions involved.

verses.text: especially because you are expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently.
verses.arminianNotes: Agrippa is an expert in Jewish customs and controversies, so Paul asks him to listen patiently.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul tailors his argument to an informed hearer, appealing to Scripture and Jewish hope rather than general philosophy.

verses.text: “Indeed, all the Jews know my way of life from my youth up, which was from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem;
verses.arminianNotes: All the Jews know how he lived from his youth among his own nation and in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: His early life was public and conventional, which makes his change all the more striking.

verses.text: having known me from the first, if they are willing to testify, that after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee.
verses.arminianNotes: They have known for a long time, if they would testify, that he lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest party of their religion.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul’s religious credentials were impeccable. Reformed writers note that this strictness did not save him; grace did.

verses.text: Now I stand here to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
verses.arminianNotes: Now he stands on trial because of his hope in the promise God made to their fathers.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul frames the gospel as the fulfillment of Israel’s own promise, not a rival to it.

verses.text: which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa!
verses.arminianNotes: The twelve tribes, worshiping earnestly night and day, hope to attain this promise, and for this hope he is accused, “O king.”
verses.reformedNotes: The irony is sharp: Paul is accused by Jews for believing what Israel itself hopes for.

verses.text: Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead?
verses.arminianNotes: “Why is it judged incredible with you if God raises the dead?” Paul turns from defense to direct appeal, addressing everyone present.
verses.reformedNotes: If God is the Creator, resurrection is not beyond him. The question answers both Sadducean doubt and Greek skepticism.

verses.text: “I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul once thought he ought to do many things against the name of Jesus of Nazareth. His opposition was a matter of conviction, not mere malice.
verses.reformedNotes: Sincere conviction can be sincerely wrong. Paul’s testimony is a warning against trusting zeal without truth.

verses.text: I also did this in Jerusalem. I both shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death I gave my vote against them.
verses.arminianNotes: He imprisoned many saints with authority from the chief priests and cast his vote against them when they were put to death.
verses.reformedNotes: The phrase “I cast my vote” may be literal or figurative; either way Paul owns his share in the deaths of believers.

verses.text: Punishing them often in all the synagogues, I tried to make them blaspheme. Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities.
verses.arminianNotes: He punished them often in all the synagogues, tried to make them blaspheme, and, raging against them, pursued them even to foreign cities.
verses.reformedNotes: The confession heightens the mercy that follows. Paul never minimizes what he was.

verses.text: “Whereupon as I traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission from the chief priests,
verses.arminianNotes: On one such mission to Damascus he traveled with authority and commission from the chief priests.
verses.reformedNotes: He was acting as an official agent of the very council now accusing him.

verses.text: at noon, O king, I saw on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those who traveled with me.
verses.arminianNotes: At midday, “O king,” he saw a light from heaven brighter than the sun, shining around him and his companions.
verses.reformedNotes: Each telling heightens the light. Here it surpasses the noonday sun, a sign of divine glory.

verses.text: When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’
verses.arminianNotes: All fell to the ground, and he heard a voice in Hebrew: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.” Arminian readers often take the proverb to mean that Saul had been resisting God’s promptings, a resistance that was painful but not yet final.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the goads as God’s pressure on Saul’s conscience, which he could not ultimately escape. The proverb describes the futility of opposing God.

verses.text: “I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ “He said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
verses.arminianNotes: “Who are you, Lord?” “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”
verses.reformedNotes: The same exchange in all three accounts is the fixed center of Paul’s testimony.

verses.text: But arise, and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things which you have seen and of the things which I will reveal to you;
verses.arminianNotes: “Get up and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you to appoint you a servant and a witness.” The language recalls the commissioning of Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:1).
verses.reformedNotes: This version compresses Ananias’s message into Jesus’ own words. The appointment comes directly from the risen Lord.

verses.text: delivering you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you,
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus promises to rescue Paul from his own people and from the Gentiles, to whom he is sending him.
verses.reformedNotes: The promise of rescue stands behind every escape Luke has narrated, including this very hearing.

verses.text: to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’
verses.arminianNotes: Paul is sent to open their eyes, to turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, so they may receive forgiveness and a share among those sanctified by faith in Jesus. Arminian theologians read the opening of eyes as the work of preaching and grace that enables people to turn, while the turning remains their own act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed theologians point to the language of Isaiah 42:7 and see the preached word as God’s instrument for giving sight to the blind. They note that the inheritance belongs to those “sanctified by faith in me,” tying the whole process to union with Christ.
